headline: Medium prompt-injection and capability-conflict risk from shared skill-style workflows; no direct evidence of data leakage or compliance breach.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Agent A’s sandboxing says skills “reference each other and build on shared context,” and A can read/write files; B uses MCP and “connect once, consume everywhere,” so a shared instruction channel is plausible. No direct proof of a shared filesystem or parser, so uncertainty pushes this above low.
conditions: IF A’s skill output is ingested by B through MCP or files without provenance checks, prompt injection is reachable.
IF the orchestrator exposes shared context between A and B, attacker-controlled text can steer B.
mitigations: Disable automatic ingestion of A outputs into B.
Add provenance tags to all A-generated files.
Require a human review step before B executes instructions from A.
Restrict B MCP endpoints to read-only data sources.
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and instruction/data separation.

B_data_leakage.rationale: A touches marketing content and product marketing context, while B touches financial, licensed, and public data. The profiles do not show a shared workspace or that either agent uploads file contents by default, so leakage is possible only through an unproven bridge; uncertainty keeps this low rather than none.
conditions: IF A and B share a filesystem or mounted workspace, cross-reading of content becomes possible.
IF B’s MCP server is pointed at A’s files, A’s marketing context can leak into financial outputs.
mitigations: Separate A and B into distinct directories.
Remove any shared mounts between the agents.
Audit MCP server targets before launch.
Keep sensitive files out of A’s writable paths.
requires-engineering: enforce workspace isolation at the orchestrator level.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: A can write the filesystem and spawn subprocesses; B cannot write files or modify git state, but it can use MCP and run multiple instances. There is no direct write-write collision, yet shared mutable resources via MCP or a common workspace could still create conflicts, so the interaction is plausible but not high.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same writable directory, A can overwrite artifacts B consumes.
IF B’s MCP tools expose mutable shared resources, concurrent runs can race on those resources.
mitigations: Assign separate working directories.
Disable concurrent writes to shared resources.
Run only one instance per workspace.
Lock any shared MCP-backed resource before use.
requires-engineering: add optimistic-concurrency or locking to the orchestrator.

D_cascading_error.rationale: A’s outputs are intended to build on shared context, and B’s “connect once, consume everywhere” pattern suggests downstream reuse of upstream outputs. Because B has no documented verification step and may act on A’s text, a mistaken or manipulated A output can cascade into B’s financial outputs; the pathway is inferred, not directly observed.
conditions: IF B consumes A-generated text as authoritative input, errors can propagate into financial analysis.
IF A emits fabricated facts or citations, B may render them without verification.
mitigations: Require B to cite source data, not A summaries.
Add a verification checklist before B publishes outputs.
Flag A-generated claims as untrusted input.
Compare A outputs against raw data before use.
requires-engineering: implement automated source-grounding checks.

E_compliance.rationale: A is a marketing agent and B is a financial-modeling agent; the profiles show different data classes and no explicit residency or certification mismatch. Because no PHI, EU-only, or retention conflict is documented, compliance risk is limited to possible policy mismatch if the operator routes regulated data through both.
conditions: IF regulated financial data is routed through A’s marketing workflows, policy mismatch may occur.
IF B is used on data subject to stricter retention than A’s handling, retention controls may diverge.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of A.
Document retention rules for both agents.
Use separate data classifications per agent.
Review logs for sensitive fields before enabling sharing.
requires-engineering: add policy-based routing for regulated datasets.
